newsitem.title: UK: RTRS-FOCUS-Aluminium price tumbles to two year lows.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-Aluminium price tumbles to two year lows.

text.p: The price of aluminium tumbled to the lowest for two years on Wednesday on the London Metal Exchange (LME), sending shivers through other non-ferrous metals as well, metal analysts said.

Prices hit $1,437 a tonne as speculative investment funds sold, having lost faith in the market with metal demand slow. Aluminium prices were last at these levels in August 1994, when the whole market was at the start of a blistering commodity market rally. It reached $2,195 a tonne in January 1995, and was as high as $1,700 at the start of this year.

Copper slumped as well and other LME metals followed suit, as the end of summer and post-Sumitomo blues soured investor feeling towards the metals complex which reached its high-water mark for the current cycle at the start of 1996.
"Generally, it is just sentiment...but aluminium has led the way down," said analyst Jim Lennon of brokers Macquarie Equities Ltd.

Aluminium has been declining gradually over recent weeks from levels above $1,500, with the slide hastening this week as what consumer interest there is was not enough to hold prices. Also, a major industry conference in Germany earlier this week failed to generate much enthusiasm for the market, as there was little discussion about a recovery in demand, Lennon noted.
Meanwhile, LME metal inventories rose 4,700 tonnes on Tuesday, while a fall in producer stocks in July was below previous declines, sending sell-signals to some traders.

"It (the decline) is stale bull liquidation as people are becoming less and less convinced about the market. LME stocks are still building, the IPA figures were disappointing, and that was enough to push it over the edge," Angus MacMillan, analyst at LME broker Billiton Metals said.
Its outlook is not looking too good either, as demand has not risen after the summer slowdowns in the Western Hemisphere, analysts noted.

"Demand simply has not picked up, and the longer consumers delay the larger the stock overhang will be," MacMillan said. Economic prospects are at best mixed for aluminium and the other industrial metals. There is good growth in the U.S. economy, but the Fed is likely to step in and cool things down by raising rates late this year.
Meanwhile in Europe the need to meet convergence criteria for monetary union in the Continental economies is expected to dampen growth prospects for 1997.
"We are looking at growth next year of 1.50 percent, which does not translate into great metal demand," MacMillan said.
Copper prices dived perilously close to the $1,900 level on the LME, touching a one-month low of $1,905, with the market still suffering a Sumitomo Corp hangover.

Prices touched $2,715 in May, but a month later the firing of Sumitomo's head trader Yasuo Hamanaka after he ran up losses of $1.8 billion in unauthorised trading over 10 years sounded the death-knell for copper's long bull-run.
And with both aluminium and copper on the defensive, the other LME metals are on the retreat.

The recent best performer nickel briefly hit a 2-1/2 month high of $7,850 on Wednesday after a furnace explosion at an Inco operation in Indonesia, but then scampered back to $7,650. Zinc backed away from above $1,020 and may now be heading for the $1,000 level.
Tin and lead, reasonably steady recently, were also heading lower.
